- **Using AI to keep working late.** The routine is a closing tool, not an extra work session.
- **Harsh self-review.** Criticism drains motivation. Notice, learn and move on.
- **Sharing sensitive details.** Keep AI inputs general.
- **Only doing it when you feel organised.** The routine matters most on chaotic days.

## Next steps

Set a reminder for a ten-minute shutdown at the end of your next work session and try the prompt once. Find companion templates in the [productivity prompts](/prompts/category/productivity), plan longer-term study goals with the [Study Planner](/study-planner), and build your own closing prompt with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder).

faq.q: What is a shutdown routine?
faq.a: A shutdown routine is a short set of steps at the end of your workday that closes open loops, captures unfinished tasks and sets up tomorrow. It helps you stop thinking about work and rest more fully in the evening.

faq.q: How long should an end-of-day routine take?
faq.a: Ten minutes is enough for most people, and five works on busy days. The goal is a reliable ritual, not a perfect review. If it grows beyond fifteen minutes, trim the steps until it feels easy to repeat.

faq.q: Can AI help me wind down after work?
faq.a: It can help you organise tasks, write a quick reflection and draft tomorrow's plan. It should not keep you working late. Treat the routine as a closing ritual and avoid opening new tasks once it is finished.

faq.q: Should I plan tomorrow at night or in the morning?
faq.a: Planning at the end of the day lets you start tomorrow quickly and relieves nighttime worry about forgotten tasks. You can make a small adjustment in the morning if things changed. Many people find this combination works best.

title: Plan Around Your Energy, Not Just Your Time, with AI
excerpt: Match tasks to your natural energy rhythm. Track simple patterns for a week, then use AI to build a schedule that puts the right work in the right hours.
seo_title: Plan Around Your Energy, Not Just Your Time, with AI
seo_description: Learn to plan your work around energy, not just time. Track your rhythm for a week, then use AI to match hard, easy and creative tasks to the right hours.
content:
Planning around energy means noticing when you tend to think clearly, when you slump and when you are best at creative or routine work, then placing tasks accordingly. AI can help you spot patterns in a week of simple notes and build a schedule that fits, but your own observations are the real data.

Most schedules treat every hour as equal. In reality, an hour of analysis at your sharpest is worth far more than the same hour when you are exhausted. A modest shift, like moving the hardest task to your best window, can improve your work without adding a minute.

## Energy is more than sleep

Energy is influenced by many things: sleep, food, movement, stress, light, social demands and the nature of the task itself. It is also not fixed. A poor night, an exam week or a change of routine can shift it.

This guide does not make medical claims. If you have ongoing fatigue, sleep problems or health concerns, consult a qualified professional. Here we are only concerned with practical scheduling based on your own observations.

## Step 1: Track for one to two weeks

You need simple data. Three times a day, such as mid-morning, early afternoon and early evening, note:

- **Energy:** 1 (very low) to 5 (high).
- **Focus:** 1 to 5.
- **What you were doing.**
- **Anything unusual:** poor sleep, heavy meal, stressful call.

Keep it to ten seconds per entry. A note on your phone or a small table on paper is plenty. The goal is rough patterns, not scientific precision.

## Step 2: Find your patterns with AI

After a week or two, paste your anonymised log into a prompt:

```
Here is a log of my energy and focus ratings with times and
activities: [paste].

Please:
1. Identify when my energy and focus tend to be highest and lowest.
2. Note any patterns linked to activities, meals or sleep that I
   mentioned.
3. Say how confident you are, given the small amount of data.
4. Suggest two small experiments I could try next week.
Do not give medical advice or diagnoses.
```

The request for confidence matters. Two weeks of notes can suggest trends but not certainties. Treat the findings as hypotheses to test.

## Step 3: Classify your tasks

Sort your regular work into types:

- **Deep tasks:** need concentration, such as writing, analysis, studying new concepts or problem solving.
- **Shallow tasks:** routine and low-stakes, such as admin, scheduling and quick replies.
- **Creative tasks:** brainstorming and design, which some people do best when slightly relaxed.
- **Social tasks:** meetings, calls and collaboration.
- **Recovery:** breaks, movement and meals.

Then match types to energy windows. For many people, deep tasks fit high-focus hours, shallow tasks fit slumps and social tasks fit moderate energy. Your own pattern may differ, so use your data, not generalisations.

## Step 4: Build an energy-aware schedule

```
Build a schedule for [day/week] using my energy pattern.

My pattern: high focus [hours], medium [hours], low [hours].
Fixed commitments: [list].
Tasks with type and estimate:
- [task] - [deep/shallow/creative/social] - [time]

Rules:
- Place deep tasks in my high-focus hours.
- Put shallow tasks and admin in low-energy hours.
- Include short breaks, a proper meal time, and 20% buffer.
- If a deep task cannot fit in my high hours, tell me and suggest
  options.
```

Compare the result with your reality. If many meetings sit in your best hours, consider asking to move some or protecting at least one block. Our guide to time blocking on the [Promptzyra blog](/blog) covers the scheduling side in more detail.

## Step 5: Use energy-friendly tactics

- **Start with the hardest task** if your best hours come first.
- **Use short walks or stretching** between blocks.
- **Eat and hydrate regularly.** Heavy meals can make some people sleepy, so notice your own response.
- **Take real breaks** away from screens.
- **Plan lighter evenings** after demanding days.
- **Keep a low-energy list** of useful, easy tasks for flat moments.

Ask AI to generate a low-energy menu for you:

```
Create a list of 10 useful tasks I can do when I am tired and
unfocused, based on my usual work: [describe]. Each should take under
20 minutes and need little mental effort.
```

Keep the list visible so you do not waste low-energy time on guilt.

### Students and shift workers

Students with changing timetables can map their energy across a typical week. Place the hardest revision in your best available slots, and use the [Study Planner](/study-planner) to build around fixed classes. Shift workers or carers with irregular hours can track patterns by shift type, not by clock time, and plan accordingly.

### Review and adjust

Every few weeks, repeat a short tracking period or review your weekly notes. Ask: Did the schedule help? Which tasks still feel heavy? What changed in my routine? Energy patterns shift with seasons, workloads and life events, so treat your schedule as living.

Combine energy planning with your weekly review. If a task keeps being postponed, the reason may be a mismatch between task and time, not a lack of discipline.

### A small experiment to try this week

Choose one change and test it for five working days. For example, move your single most demanding task to the first ninety minutes of your day and keep messages for later. Record how the task went, how you felt afterwards and whether anything unexpected got in the way. At the end of the week, compare it with the previous week.

If the change helped, keep it and test another. If it did not, return to your old pattern and try a different adjustment. Treat every change as a cheap experiment, not a permanent rule. Over a few months, these small tests add up to a schedule that fits you far better than any template could.

## Common mistakes

- **Copying someone else's ideal routine.** Your rhythm may differ from a famous early riser's.
- **Ignoring fixed constraints.** Work with the hours you actually have.
- **Over-trusting AI analysis of tiny data.** Two weeks suggests trends, not facts.
- **Scheduling hard work after long meeting blocks.** Protect a few focus windows.
- **Skipping breaks and meals.** Pushing through often reduces quality.
- **Making medical conclusions.** Leave health questions to professionals.
- **Overcomplicating tracking.** Simple ratings are enough.
- **Expecting constant high energy.** Everyone has low periods. Plan for them kindly.

faq.q: What does planning around energy mean?
faq.a: It means scheduling demanding tasks when you tend to feel alert and saving easier work for lower-energy periods. Instead of treating all hours as equal, you use your natural rhythm to get better results with less strain.

faq.q: How do I find my peak energy times?
faq.a: Track your energy and focus a few times a day for one to two weeks, noting the task and a simple 1 to 5 rating. Patterns usually emerge. Remember that sleep, food, stress and routine can shift your rhythm.

faq.q: Can AI tell me my chronotype?
faq.a: No. It can help you analyse your own notes and spot patterns, but it cannot measure your biology. Any conclusions are rough guides. For sleep or health concerns, speak to a qualified healthcare professional.

faq.q: What if my schedule is fixed by work or school?
faq.a: Work within your constraints. Use your best available hours for the most demanding tasks, place easier work in lower-energy periods and add short breaks. Small adjustments, like moving one task, can still make a difference.
